newsitem.title: USA: CME hogs end limit up on Taiwan ban, bellies mixed.
newsitem.headline: CME hogs end limit up on Taiwan ban, bellies mixed.

text.p: The Taiwan pork export ban continued to hold nearby CME hog futures up the daily limit at the close, but gains in deferred months were pared by profit taking, traders said.
Pork bellies closed mixed but mostly lower on an overbought condition and concern that recent high cash prices would cut off demand, floor sources said.

April and June hogs closed up the daily 2.000-cent-a-lb limit with April at 74.275 cents. Other months ended 1.825 to 0.850 cent higher. Pork bellies retreated to close 0.500 cent a lb higher to 1.050 lower with only March up and May off 0.450 at 78.850 cents.
April and December hog contracts were the only months that failed to post new contract highs on the advance, sources noted.

Values rose and hit buy stops, sparked by expectations U.S. pork will to a large extent, replace Taiwan pork in Pacific Rim countries. Such ideas sparked a jump in prices since last Thursday. Taiwan halted pork exports because of an outbreak of foot and mouth disease in hogs and their main export customers have also halted imports until further notice.
Speculation is that it could take more than a year before the foot and mouth disease is cleared up there and exports resume, traders said.
April still had 600 buy orders unfilled at the close but the market started to run into profit taking, especially in back months, they said.

"If you look at the fundamentals we've probably got a ways to go, but they need some profit taking - they need some retracement," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
"(Futures) are way at a sharp premium," Benson added.
The latest CME lean hog index was quoted at $66.48 per cwt on Friday compared with Monday's April hog contract close at 74.275 cents a lb.
Analysts noted that Thursday's quarterly USDA Hog and Pigs report will have to show increased hog numbers to provide meaningful resistance to pork markets.

Analysts' early estimates on the report were ranging from 97 to 100.6 percent of a year ago for all U.S. hogs. Hogs kept for breeding were estimated at 98.5 to 104 percent of a year ago and hogs kept for market at 97 to 100.8 percent.
In hog options, volatility was up one to two percent across the board. Commission houses sold 72 and 74 April calls and bought June 82 and 84 calls and October 74 calls, pit sources said.

Pork belly futures were buoyed by the Taiwan situation early, but slipped as demand in that pit waned. The market appeared overbought and ran out of support, especially with cash prices recently climbing to levels that found heavy consumer resistance previously, traders said.
"They are more sensitive to high prices shutting down demand," said Julia Bussie, livestock analyst for AG Edwards.

The large basis that futures held also encouraged storings. Demand from the Taiwan situation was boosting belly futures faster than cash belly prices and prompting larger movement into cold storage. Also, bacon is not one of the items that would be heavily in demand from the Taiwan export stoppage, sources said.
"It's not as bullish for pork bellies," said Jim Clarkson, analyst for A and A Inc.
R.J. O'Brien and LFG sold along with locals after early buying from Cargill Investor Services, pit sources added.
